name: Streptococcosis
cause: other Streptococcus species associated with tilapia disease
visual_signs: haemorrhage around the eyes, operculum, mouth, vent, or fin bases
water_quality_associations: poor water quality may increase susceptibility by stressing fish
conflicting_evidence: surface gasping without neurological or ocular signs may be better explained by low dissolved oxygen
skin or gill patches are more characteristic of columnaris
confirmation_methods: Gram stain of fresh internal tissue
bacterial culture and identification from internal organs, especially brain and kidney
safe_actions: contact an aquatic veterinarian or fish-health laboratory
escalation_triggers: multiple fish with eye haemorrhage or pop-eye

name: Motile Aeromonas Septicemia
visual_signs: haemorrhaged or inflamed fins and skin
water_quality_associations: poor water quality may stress fish and increase susceptibility to opportunistic infection
conflicting_evidence: frayed fins with pale necrotic gill lesions may fit columnaris better
circling with eye haemorrhage and rapid mortality may fit streptococcosis
surface gasping affecting most fish suddenly may indicate water-quality stress
confirmation_methods: bacterial culture from kidney or other affected internal organs
laboratory identification of the bacterial isolate
safe_actions: check dissolved oxygen, ammonia, nitrite, pH, and temperature
submit suitable fish to a diagnostic laboratory before treatment
escalation_triggers: loss of equilibrium in multiple fish

name: Columnaris disease
visual_signs: irregular whitish-to-grey patches on skin or fins
behavioral_signs: respiratory distress may occur when gills are affected
reduced activity may occur in sick fish
water_quality_associations: water chemistry and recent stressors should be checked because environmental problems and infection can occur together
conflicting_evidence: neurological swimming and eye haemorrhage are more characteristic of streptococcosis
generalised haemorrhage and abdominal swelling may fit septicemia or TiLV better
gasping without visible gill damage may be environmental
confirmation_methods: examination of fresh skin, fin, and gill samples
assessment of water quality and coexisting disease
safe_actions: photograph skin, fin, and gill findings
contact a fish-health laboratory for confirmation
escalation_triggers: rapid spread of skin or gill lesions

name: Tilapia Lake Virus disease
affected_species: other susceptible tilapine species and hybrids
visual_signs: skin erosion or haemorrhagic skin lesions
water_quality_associations: clinical signs are non-specific, so water-quality causes must be evaluated rather than assumed normal
risk_factors: movement or transfer of fish between ponds
exposure to infected farmed or wild fish populations
conflicting_evidence: clinical signs alone cannot confirm TiLV
isolated surface gasping with abnormal dissolved oxygen may be environmental
classic frayed fins and grey skin patches may fit columnaris better
confirmation_methods: RT-PCR or RT-qPCR performed by a qualified laboratory
virus isolation or other validated laboratory methods
safe_actions: contact aquatic animal-health authorities or a qualified laboratory
escalation_triggers: multiple fish with ocular and skin abnormalities

name: Water-quality stress
visual_signs: there may be few disease-specific external lesions
behavioral_signs: crowding near water inlets or aeration
water_quality_associations: FAO training material gives an optimum dissolved oxygen value above 5 mg/L for Nile tilapia
the same source gives an optimum unionised ammonia (NH3) value below 0.1 mg/L
pH changes alter the toxic fraction of ammonia
conflicting_evidence: normal measurements taken at the time of distress weaken a purely environmental explanation
progressive disease-specific lesions or mortality confined to part of the stock may suggest an infectious cause
normal water quality does not exclude an earlier transient event
confirmation_methods: measure dissolved oxygen immediately, including near dawn when relevant
test ammonia, nitrite, pH, and temperature
review aeration, filtration, feeding, stocking, and recent water changes
investigate infection if signs persist after water conditions are corrected
safe_actions: restore or increase aeration when low oxygen is suspected
stop avoidable handling and record readings
seek farm or veterinary guidance before chemical or drug treatment
escalation_triggers: very low dissolved oxygen or unsafe ammonia/nitrite reading
rapid mortality across much of the population
